Atlanta, Georgia

believe that he had 2 game wins going in.

There are too many masters thanks to some last minute card additions.
The Rampage really ought to be an Arson, but Rampage is so much
cooler. I never got to use Destructive Secrets, but I think it would
be quite good in an end game. The deck can wrestle for vote control
with the "I (re)vote my Nos Justicar, it passes easily, Cryptic Rider,
Praxis Seizure" trick. I had fun stealing Living Manse and Palatial
Estate with Disputed Territory. Club Zombie's intercept is meant to be
given to Embraces to block nasty actions, or it's just an expensive
hunting ground. When the deck is up and running well, it tends to lots
of vamps and pool. Special thanks to Will Kristoff, Nick Smith, and
Mark Loughman for loaning me cards to complete my deck.

-----------------------------------------

DragonCon 2004
Atlanta, Georgia
September 5th, 2004
16 players
2R + F

Jeffrey Thompson won using this deck with 4 victory points in every
round, including the finals. Only 1 victory point was acquired via
Dramatic Upheaval, that happened in the first round. This was the
same deck he played at the North American Continental Championship
where he also took 1 game win.

Deck Name: A Sudden Anarch Troublemaker
Created By: The Lasombra
Description: Get the Anarch Troublemaker in play early. Use it on the
turn you expect to finish your prey, or on a turn where it will make a
big enough difference that you can afford to have it used by your
prey. Optimally, you will play another one on the turn you give it to
your prey to prevent them from using it should they survive your
attack. Sudden Reversal is key to preventing other decks from
destroying you or your strategy. Successful Sudden targets included
Minion Taps, Blood Dolls, Fame, and Ventrue Headquarters.

Messages.Author: David Cherryholmes
Messages.Body:
LSJ wrote:

> "practically" wasn't in there.

I don't believe there is a difference between "practically" and "in
practice". If there is a subtle semantic difference, it is not
important to the point I'm trying to make, and I believe you understand
my intent.

> Your assertion, "play to win is unenforceable in practice," is the one
> that derailed the thread into the thread at hand.

> Play to win is enforceable in practice. It has been enforced in practice,
> in fact.

I'm sure examples can be produced where it has been enforced. After
all, we both agree that a simple exercise in judgment is all that it
takes to enforce it. But in most cases where one would think playing to
win is in question, it is left to the player's self-determination
whether he is playing to win or not, and it is trivial to satisfy that
condition in order to play to lose.

> His statement that he was not playing to win was in error -- he, like
> others, is free to choose his words poorly or to engage in ire-raising
> as he sees fit.

On what grounds do you not take his statement at face value? If saying
you aren't playing to win, and then going on to conclude the game having
taken no steps to play to win.... if those conditions aren't sufficient
to enforce the rule, then I conclude again that it is practically
unenforceable.

> As it was explained to me, his situation was lost and he chose to
> lose in one manner over another.

That's the problem. All you have to do is decide for yourself "my
position is lost", and the door swings wide open to not play to win. He
had 30 pool. Plenty of minion taps to make the consequences of
torporing any given instance of Anson minimal. Plenty of Golcondas to
foil Contracts and Fame. Anthelios to recycle them. IMO, he still had
a perfectly reasonable chance to win the game. However, that is the
crux, isn't it? It's not my determination, nor even yours as a judge
(again, practically.... in most cases judges will yield their own
judgments to the judgment of the player in question).

> This is not an example of a
> violation of play to win, so, if the situation was explained to
> me properly, you are correct that I would not have stepped in
> and changed a legal play.

Your definition of "properly" is a loaded one. If he says he isn't
playing to win and acts that way, what more do you need? Are you
suggesting you put words in his mouth to the effect of "what you really
mean is [x]"?

--

David Cherryholmes

> > As it was explained to me, his situation was lost and he chose to
> > lose in one manner over another.
>
> That's the problem. All you have to do is decide for yourself "my
> position is lost", and the door swings wide open to not play to win. He

Not true. You have to convince the judge (assuming not all of the
players at the table agree with your decision, and one of the
dissenters calls for a judge).

> had 30 pool. Plenty of minion taps to make the consequences of
> torporing any given instance of Anson minimal. Plenty of Golcondas to
> foil Contracts and Fame. Anthelios to recycle them. IMO, he still had

> crux, isn't it? It's not my determination, nor even yours as a judge
> (again, practically.... in most cases judges will yield their own
> judgments to the judgment of the player in question).

Not true. If a judge had been called, it would then have been the
judge's determination. Once the judge is called, the players'
determination is irrelevant.

> > This is not an example of a
> > violation of play to win, so, if the situation was explained to
> > me properly, you are correct that I would not have stepped in
> > and changed a legal play.
>
> Your definition of "properly" is a loaded one. If he says he isn't
> playing to win and acts that way, what more do you need? Are you

He didn't act that way (as explained to me), as I noted.

> suggesting you put words in his mouth to the effect of "what you really
> mean is [x]"?

No. I'm suggesting that a player who cannot win and who misstates
his actions in that regard as not playing to win (either because
he doesn't understand the ins and outs of the play to win rule or
because he wants the reaction such a statement will garner) is
still in the "cannot win" position.

This applies uniformly in both cases -- the player's judgment of
his adherence or violation of the play to win rule is not what
matters -- it's the judge's judgment that matters.

A few quick notes:
--minion taps would be useless in this case, as Anson would enter
torpor empty, courtesy Fatima's Assault Rifle.
--Golconda would indeed reclaim pool, assuming some supporting
weenie didn't diablerize Anson in the same turn as the torporization.

> foil Contracts and Fame. Anthelios to recycle them. IMO, he still had
> a perfectly reasonable chance to win the game. However, that is the
> crux, isn't it? It's not my determination, nor even yours as a judge
> (again, practically.... in most cases judges will yield their own

Not only is it a judgement call in this case, it's verifiable by the
decklists. If there's no combat defense, there's no chance to get a
VP, much less a win. Let's see 'em! :-)

>
> > This is not an example of a
> > violation of play to win, so, if the situation was explained to
> > me properly, you are correct that I would not have stepped in
> > and changed a legal play.
>
> Your definition of "properly" is a loaded one. If he says he isn't
> playing to win and acts that way, what more do you need? Are you
> suggesting you put words in his mouth to the effect of "what you really
> mean is [x]"?

Not only is the situation not an example of a violation, it's always
been a valid defense against dedicated combat. And specifically
toward the unicycle combat decks: I think they formerly were 0-VP
decks, and with cards like Dragonbound and Tension, they're now 1-VP
decks. A prey either hoses the unicycle or gets run over by it. In
the case of being run over, bringing vampires out only hands the
combat deck a VP.

As a counterpoint: I could have, arguably should have, done the same
thing in round 1. My game was lost the moment Fatima hit the table.
Instead of diablerizing vamp A with vamp B, and attempting to pass the
bloodhunt, I chose to suicide forward instead, using our 2-turn deal
to buy myself some actions. I knew Robyn (your pred., my grand-pred)
would sit on Anachronism (or similar hoser) until I was ousted, so
there was no benefit to me sitting there. I then tried to throw as
much momentum to your unicycle as possible.

You had two of three rounds in which you had a prey dead to rights.
One gave you a VP and 6-9 pool damage toward your next prey. One
played dead and made you work for it. I think either course is legal
for a dead-duck prey.

point that brings me to admit he was playing to win as best he could,
given his position. However, when I said "he had 30 pool", I didn't
mean the same thirty the rest of us start with. He'd brought Anson out
a few times already, put many permenants into play, taken as many chump
bleeds as I could send his way, and was still back up to 30. My point?
You will take some lumps from your predator. If, in the course of
pursuing ousting his prey, he lost 8 pool.... to me, that is just the
normal course of the game, not a reason to put it in park.

> Not only is the situation not an example of a violation, it's always
> been a valid defense against dedicated combat. And specifically
> toward the unicycle combat decks: I think they formerly were 0-VP
> decks, and with cards like Dragonbound and Tension, they're now 1-VP
> decks. A prey either hoses the unicycle or gets run over by it. In
> the case of being run over, bringing vampires out only hands the
> combat deck a VP.

And not bringing out vampires hands yourself 0 VP and someone else the
game. It would be nice if we had the luxury of just denying our
predator the ability to bleed us by refusing to play, but we don't, so
everyone accepts that fact. Unfortunately, combat decks can be unwound
and stymied with very little effort.

However, I don't think they are "1 VP decks". If every prey you get
knee-jerks and says "fuck it" and waits out your death, then sure....
you both lose. The fact that many, many players will do this at the
drop of a hat doesn't, to me, immediately equate to the deck being bad
so much as players lacking the nuts to go for it. And barring getting
sandwiched between the combat that trumps yours (in my case, Animalism),
or someone who has brought a one vampire trick deck that has no answer
whatsoever to combat with an 8 cap, I still think it comes down to a
game of cards that could go any which way. One of the great things
about this game is that you always have more than one player to worry
about (unless, of course, one of the players at the table isn't playing).

> As a counterpoint: I could have, arguably should have, done the same
> thing in round 1. My game was lost the moment Fatima hit the table.
> Instead of diablerizing vamp A with vamp B, and attempting to pass the
> bloodhunt, I chose to suicide forward instead, using our 2-turn deal
> to buy myself some actions. I knew Robyn (your pred., my grand-pred)
> would sit on Anachronism (or similar hoser) until I was ousted, so
> there was no benefit to me sitting there. I then tried to throw as
> much momentum to your unicycle as possible.

Actually, it looked to me like she sat there until you were ousted
because that was the point at which Dave said "I won't touch you, get
him". But IMO you made the competitive play. Fatima is a fragile deck,
and all it would have taken is one bad DotB combat and I would be gone.
You had vampires that could have been rescued from torpor and up and
running. Had you sat there, it would have taken longer to get back in
the game if Fatima had taken the dirt nap. Anyway, it's a game of
limited information, but I'd rather have a hand in so I can take
advantage of an opportunity.

> You had two of three rounds in which you had a prey dead to rights.
> One gave you a VP and 6-9 pool damage toward your next prey. One
> played dead and made you work for it. I think either course is legal
> for a dead-duck prey.

Yeah, but you weren't a dead duck prey. Don't you have Majesties?
Maybe some prevent? I guess people are imagining my build of Fatima as
being a certain kill, but IME it doesn't play out that way.

--

David Cherryholmes

Messages.Author: David Cherryholmes

> Correct. And what is the sense in constantly reclaiming the 8 pool you just
> spend ?!? Beside that I hoped that you would start attacking Jay´s vampires

I did rush him, twice. He DI'd my Freak Drive, twice. And this was

> The appearance of Democritus would then have allowed my to play some of the

> the game was really that I didn´t cycle into a Recruitment, and I tried hard

This satisfies me that you were playing to win, for whatever it's worth.

David Cherryholmes

Messages.Author: David Cherryholmes
Messages.Body:
Johannes Walch wrote:

> And before you complain, David, that I was no predator to Jay, where was
> your predator? You had no predator either for the entire game and you were
> not able to oust me, even though I had much less pool than Jay and no
> defenses at all.

I had Presence bleeders behind me, who did bleed me a few times for
significant numbers, which in turn affected my allocation of resources.
Beyond that, my grandpredator was the pure Malk 1994 deck, with Ozmo
and Didi letting bleeds of 6 rip ad nauseum, and this deck could have
become me new predator on any given turn. I most certainly had a
predator that game.

As to not ousting you... c'mon man, you played Anson Golconda/Minion Tap
with no minions, I was playing non-weenie rush. And lastly, saying you
had "much less pool than Jay" is silly. Ok, so you had 25 pool instead
of his 40.
